question.text: What three steps come before passing another vehicle?

answer.text: To pass, first look ahead and behind to judge whether it is safe, then signal to the drivers around you, then sound the horn to alert the driver ahead.

teaching.text: Look ahead and behind first, then signal, then sound the horn to alert the driver ahead. Remember: look, signal, horn.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: To pass, first look ahead and behind to judge whether it is safe, then signal to the drivers around you, then sound the horn to alert the driver ahead.

question.text: What does sounding your horn before passing require of the driver ahead?

answer.text: Your horn signal puts the driver you are passing under a legal duty to help you get by.

teaching.text: Your horn signal places the driver you pass under a legal duty to help you get by. Remember: horn creates a duty.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Your horn signal puts the driver you are passing under a legal duty to help you get by.

question.text: What room, speed and sight distance do you need to pass?

answer.text: Pass only with plenty of room and a steady speed, and only if you can see far enough to get back into your lane before meeting oncoming traffic.

teaching.text: Pass only with plenty of room, a steady speed, and enough view to return before oncoming traffic. Remember: room, steady speed, clear view.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Pass only with plenty of room and a steady speed, and only if you can see far enough to get back into your lane before meeting oncoming traffic.

question.text: How much side clearance must you give the vehicle you pass?

answer.text: The law requires the passing driver to stay at least two feet to the left of the vehicle being passed.

teaching.text: Stay at least two feet to the left of the vehicle you are passing. Remember: two feet to the left.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: The law requires the passing driver to stay at least two feet to the left of the vehicle being passed.

question.text: Where is passing never safe and usually illegal?

answer.text: Railroad crossings, town and city intersections, and marked intersections in the countryside are places where passing is never safe and is usually against the law.

teaching.text: Railroad crossings, city and town intersections, and marked country intersections are never safe places to pass. Remember: no passing at crossings or intersections.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Railroad crossings, town and city intersections, and marked intersections in the countryside are places where passing is never safe and is usually against the law.
audio_scripts.must_match_memory_hook: no passing at crossings or intersections

question.text: How far ahead must you see to pass on a curve or hill?

answer.text: Do not pass on a curve or hill where you cannot see at least five hundred feet ahead.

teaching.text: On a curve or hill, do not pass unless you can see at least five hundred feet ahead. Remember: five hundred feet of sight.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Do not pass on a curve or hill where you cannot see at least five hundred feet ahead.

question.text: Which yellow line markings forbid passing?

answer.text: Do not pass where a solid yellow line is in your lane or where there is a double solid yellow line.

teaching.text: A solid yellow line in your lane, or a double solid yellow line, means no passing. Remember: solid yellow, no passing.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Do not pass where a solid yellow line is in your lane or where there is a double solid yellow line.

question.text: How do the passing clearance and the curve sight distance differ?

answer.text: Passing clearance is at least two feet to the left of the passed vehicle, while the sight distance needed to pass on a curve or hill is at least five hundred feet.

teaching.text: Clearance beside is at least two feet, while the view ahead on curves and hills must be at least five hundred feet. Remember: two feet beside, five hundred ahead.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Passing clearance is at least two feet to the left of the passed vehicle, while the sight distance needed to pass on a curve or hill is at least five hundred feet.
audio_scripts.must_match_memory_hook: two feet beside, five hundred ahead

question.text: What must you do when another driver is passing you?

answer.text: When someone is passing you, you must help: move toward the right edge if they sound the horn, and never speed up.

teaching.text: When passed, move toward the right edge if the passer sounds the horn, and never speed up. Remember: move right, never speed up.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: When someone is passing you, you must help: move toward the right edge if they sound the horn, and never speed up.

question.text: When does speeding up while being passed become a misdemeanor?

answer.text: Speeding up and failing to give way to a passing vehicle is a misdemeanor if it leads to a crash with injury or property damage.

teaching.text: Speeding up and not giving way is a misdemeanor if it leads to a crash with injury or damage. Remember: speeding up into a crash.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Speeding up and failing to give way to a passing vehicle is a misdemeanor if it leads to a crash with injury or property damage.

question.text: How do the passing driver's duties differ from the passed driver's duties?

answer.text: When passing, you signal your intention and blow the horn to alert the driver ahead; when being passed, you must help by moving to the right edge of the road if the passing driver blows the horn, and you must never increase your speed.

teaching.text: The passer signals and sounds the horn; the driver being passed moves right and holds speed. Remember: Horn blown: move right, steady.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: When passing, you signal your intention and blow the horn to alert the driver ahead; when being passed, you must help by moving to the right edge of the road if the passing driver blows the horn, and you must never increase your speed.

question.text: Is passing on the right generally allowed, and why or why not?

answer.text: Passing on the right is illegal except where specifically allowed, because it puts you on the other driver's blind side, where that car might turn right or pull over.

teaching.text: Passing on the right is illegal unless allowed, because you end up on the other driver's blind side. Remember: right side is blind side.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Passing on the right is illegal except where specifically allowed, because it puts you on the other driver's blind side, where that car might turn right or pull over.

question.text: When is passing on the right allowed?

answer.text: Passing on the right is allowed on highways with two or more lanes each way, on one-way streets, around a car in a left-turn lane, and when you are in a lane reserved for right turns.

teaching.text: Passing on the right is allowed on multi-lane highways, one-way streets, beside a left turner, and from a right-turn lane. Remember: multi-lane, one-way, turners, turn lanes.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Passing on the right is allowed on highways with two or more lanes each way, on one-way streets, around a car in a left-turn lane, and when you are in a lane reserved for right turns.

question.text: On a three-lane highway, when may you use the center lane to pass?

answer.text: On a three-lane highway you may pass only in the center lane where it is marked for passing your way, unless the car in the center lane is turning left.

teaching.text: On a three-lane highway, pass only in a center lane marked for your direction, unless that car is turning left. Remember: center lane marked your way.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: On a three-lane highway you may pass only in the center lane where it is marked for passing your way, unless the car in the center lane is turning left.

question.text: Is passing on the right always illegal?

answer.text: Passing on the right is generally illegal, but it is allowed on roads with two or more lanes each way, on one-way streets, beside a left-turning car, and from a right-turn lane.

teaching.text: The ban on passing right has listed exceptions, and outside them the ban applies. Remember: banned except listed cases.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Passing on the right is generally illegal, but it is allowed on roads with two or more lanes each way, on one-way streets, beside a left-turning car, and from a right-turn lane.

question.text: Which side of the street must you park on?

answer.text: Park on the right-hand side of the street at all times, unless it is a one-way street.

teaching.text: Always park on the right-hand side unless the street is one-way. Remember: park on the right.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Park on the right-hand side of the street at all times, unless it is a one-way street.

question.text: What should you do when pulling out of a parallel parking space?

answer.text: When pulling out of a parallel space, look for approaching traffic and signal a left turn first; the signal is not needed when parked on the left of a one-way street.

teaching.text: Look for traffic and signal left before pulling out, except when parked on the left of a one-way street. Remember: look, then signal left.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: When pulling out of a parallel space, look for approaching traffic and signal a left turn first; the signal is not needed when parked on the left of a one-way street.

question.text: Which places are you never allowed to park?

answer.text: Do not park at an intersection, in front of a driveway, or on a crosswalk, sidewalk or bridge.

teaching.text: Never park at an intersection, in front of a driveway, or on a crosswalk, sidewalk or bridge. Remember: not intersections, driveways, crosswalks.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Do not park at an intersection, in front of a driveway, or on a crosswalk, sidewalk or bridge.

question.text: How close to a cross street may you park?

answer.text: Do not park within twenty-five feet of the curb line of a cross street, or within fifteen feet of the intersecting right of way lines where there is no curb.

teaching.text: Stay twenty-five feet from a cross street curb line, or fifteen feet from right of way lines with no curb. Remember: twenty-five from the curb line.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Do not park within twenty-five feet of the curb line of a cross street, or within fifteen feet of the intersecting right of way lines where there is no curb.

question.text: How close may you park to a fire hydrant or fire station entrance?

answer.text: Do not park within fifteen feet of a fire hydrant or of a fire station entrance.

teaching.text: Stay fifteen feet from a fire hydrant or a fire station entrance. Remember: fifteen from a hydrant.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Do not park within fifteen feet of a fire hydrant or of a fire station entrance.

question.text: How do the hydrant and cross-street parking distances differ?

answer.text: The no-parking distance is fifteen feet from a fire hydrant but twenty-five feet from the curb line of a cross street, and fifteen feet from the right of way lines where there is no curb.

teaching.text: Hydrants use fifteen feet, while a cross street curb line uses twenty-five feet. Remember: hydrant fifteen, corner twenty-five.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: The no-parking distance is fifteen feet from a fire hydrant but twenty-five feet from the curb line of a cross street, and fifteen feet from the right of way lines where there is no curb.

question.text: When is parking on a highway shoulder allowed?

answer.text: Never park on the paved travel part of a highway, and parking on the shoulder is illegal unless drivers from both directions can see your vehicle for at least two hundred feet.

teaching.text: Never park on the paved travel lanes, and on a shoulder only if visible for two hundred feet both ways. Remember: seen two hundred both ways.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Never park on the paved travel part of a highway, and parking on the shoulder is illegal unless drivers from both directions can see your vehicle for at least two hundred feet.

question.text: How far from a fire or fire truck must you park, inside and outside a city?

answer.text: Keep at least one block away from a fire or fire truck inside city limits, and at least four hundred feet away outside a city, when parking.

teaching.text: Keep a block from a fire or fire truck in a city, and four hundred feet outside a city. Remember: block in town, four hundred outside.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Keep at least one block away from a fire or fire truck inside city limits, and at least four hundred feet away outside a city, when parking.
audio_scripts.must_match_memory_hook: block in town, four hundred outside

question.text: How do the fire parking buffers compare with the shoulder visibility rule?

answer.text: Near a fire or fire truck the parking buffer is one block inside city limits but four hundred feet outside a city, while a parked car on a shoulder must be visible for two hundred feet both ways.

teaching.text: Fire buffers are a block in town and four hundred feet outside, while shoulder parking needs two hundred feet of visibility. Remember: fire buffers versus shoulder sight.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Near a fire or fire truck the parking buffer is one block inside city limits but four hundred feet outside a city, while a parked car on a shoulder must be visible for two hundred feet both ways.

question.text: Where may you park in an interstate right of way?

answer.text: Parking is not allowed anywhere in an interstate right of way, except in designated areas or in an emergency.

teaching.text: No parking in an interstate right of way, except in designated areas or emergencies. Remember: interstate means no parking.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Parking is not allowed anywhere in an interstate right of way, except in designated areas or in an emergency.

question.text: Who may use a disabled parking space?

answer.text: Disabled parking spaces may be used only by a vehicle showing a disability license plate or placard.

teaching.text: Only vehicles showing a disability plate or placard may use disabled spaces. Remember: plate or placard only.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Disabled parking spaces may be used only by a vehicle showing a disability license plate or placard.

question.text: What should you check before getting in to back up?

answer.text: Before getting in to back up, check behind the vehicle for children or small objects, which are hard to see from the driver's seat.

teaching.text: Check behind the vehicle for children or small objects before you get in to back up. Remember: look behind first.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Before getting in to back up, check behind the vehicle for children or small objects, which are hard to see from the driver's seat.

question.text: How should you steer and look while backing?

answer.text: When backing, steer with your left hand and look over your right shoulder through the rear window instead of relying only on the mirrors or side window.

teaching.text: Steer with your left hand and look over your right shoulder through the rear window. Remember: right shoulder, rear window.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: When backing, steer with your left hand and look over your right shoulder through the rear window instead of relying only on the mirrors or side window.

question.text: How fast may you back up?

answer.text: Back up very slowly, at no more than ten miles per hour, because a vehicle is harder to control and stop in reverse.

teaching.text: Back at no more than ten miles per hour, since a vehicle is harder to control and stop in reverse. Remember: ten or slower in reverse.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Back up very slowly, at no more than ten miles per hour, because a vehicle is harder to control and stop in reverse.

question.text: Which backing speed and look direction go together?

answer.text: The backing speed limit of no more than ten miles per hour pairs with the rule to look over the right shoulder through the rear window, not just in the mirrors.

teaching.text: Keep backing to ten or less and look back through the rear window, not only the mirrors. Remember: slow, and look back.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: The backing speed limit of no more than ten miles per hour pairs with the rule to look over the right shoulder through the rear window, not just in the mirrors.

question.text: Where do crashes happen most often?

answer.text: Intersections are where crashes happen most often, and over one-third of fatal motor vehicle crashes occur there.

teaching.text: Crashes happen most at intersections, including over one-third of fatal crashes. Remember: intersections are crash zones.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Intersections are where crashes happen most often, and over one-third of fatal motor vehicle crashes occur there.

question.text: When does a divided highway crossing count as two intersections?

answer.text: On a four-lane highway divided by a median wider than thirty feet, each crossing counts as a separate intersection.

teaching.text: With a median wider than thirty feet on a four-lane highway, each crossing is its own intersection. Remember: wide median, two intersections.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: On a four-lane highway divided by a median wider than thirty feet, each crossing counts as a separate intersection.

question.text: Must you slow down approaching an intersection even with the right of way?

answer.text: The law requires you to slow down as you approach an intersection, even when you have the right of way.

teaching.text: Slow down approaching any intersection, even with the right of way. Remember: slow down anyway.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: The law requires you to slow down as you approach an intersection, even when you have the right of way.

question.text: Does having the right of way excuse you from slowing or avoiding a crash?

answer.text: Having the right of way still requires you to slow down approaching the intersection and to avoid hitting anyone.

teaching.text: Right of way still means slowing down and avoiding anyone in your path. Remember: right of way is not permission.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Having the right of way still requires you to slow down approaching the intersection and to avoid hitting anyone.
audio_scripts.must_match_memory_hook: right of way is not permission

question.text: At an uncontrolled intersection, who goes before a car that has not entered?

answer.text: At an intersection with no signs or signals, a vehicle already inside the intersection goes before one that has not entered.

teaching.text: With no signs or signals, a vehicle already in the intersection goes first. Remember: inside goes first.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: At an intersection with no signs or signals, a vehicle already inside the intersection goes before one that has not entered.

question.text: Two vehicles reach an uncontrolled intersection at the same moment. Who goes first?

answer.text: When vehicles reach an uncontrolled intersection at the same moment, the vehicle on the right has the right of way.

teaching.text: Arriving together at an uncontrolled intersection, the vehicle on the right goes first. Remember: yield to the right.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: When vehicles reach an uncontrolled intersection at the same moment, the vehicle on the right has the right of way.

question.text: Two facing vehicles arrive together and one turns left. Who goes first?

answer.text: When two facing vehicles arrive together and one wants to turn left, the turning driver must signal and wait, so the driver going straight has the right of way.

teaching.text: Facing vehicles arriving together: the left turner signals and waits for straight traffic. Remember: left turner waits.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: When two facing vehicles arrive together and one wants to turn left, the turning driver must signal and wait, so the driver going straight has the right of way.

question.text: What is the order of right of way at an uncontrolled intersection?

answer.text: At an uncontrolled intersection the car already inside goes first, and when two arrive together the car on the right goes first; facing cars split straight-versus-left, with the left turner waiting.

teaching.text: Inside first, then the vehicle on the right, and facing left turners wait for straight traffic. Remember: inside, right, then straight.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: At an uncontrolled intersection the car already inside goes first, and when two arrive together the car on the right goes first; facing cars split straight-versus-left, with the left turner waiting.

question.text: May you change lanes while going straight through an intersection?

answer.text: Never change lanes while driving straight through an intersection.

teaching.text: Never change lanes while going straight through an intersection. Remember: no lane changes inside.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Never change lanes while driving straight through an intersection.

question.text: What must you do at a stop sign?

answer.text: At a stop sign you must stop completely and yield to traffic on the through street before moving on or turning.

teaching.text: Stop completely at a stop sign and yield to through traffic before moving. Remember: full stop, then yield.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: At a stop sign you must stop completely and yield to traffic on the through street before moving on or turning.

question.text: What must you do when leaving a private driveway or at a blind unmarked intersection?

answer.text: When coming out of a private driveway, stop and yield to every vehicle and pedestrian, and at a blind unmarked intersection stop and then creep forward carefully.

teaching.text: Stop and yield to everyone when leaving a driveway, and creep forward at a blind unmarked intersection. Remember: stop, yield, creep forward.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: When coming out of a private driveway, stop and yield to every vehicle and pedestrian, and at a blind unmarked intersection stop and then creep forward carefully.

question.text: What is a single-point interchange?

answer.text: A single-point interchange merges two intersections into one above or below a free-flowing road, run by a single set of traffic signals.

teaching.text: A single-point interchange combines two intersections into one, run by one set of signals. Remember: one signal, two intersections.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: A single-point interchange merges two intersections into one above or below a free-flowing road, run by a single set of traffic signals.

question.text: How does a modern roundabout differ from a traffic circle?

answer.text: A modern roundabout is much smaller than an older traffic circle and keeps speeds low, about fifteen to twenty miles per hour, which makes it safer.

teaching.text: Modern roundabouts are smaller than traffic circles and keep speeds around fifteen to twenty miles per hour. Remember: smaller and slower.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: A modern roundabout is much smaller than an older traffic circle and keeps speeds low, about fifteen to twenty miles per hour, which makes it safer.

question.text: Which way do you travel in a traffic circle, and how do you exit?

answer.text: In a traffic circle all vehicles travel counterclockwise to the right and leave by turning right; with more than one lane, get into the outside lane before your exit and never turn right from an inside lane.

teaching.text: Circles run counterclockwise with right-turn exits; move to the outside lane before exiting. Remember: counterclockwise, exit right.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: In a traffic circle all vehicles travel counterclockwise to the right and leave by turning right; with more than one lane, get into the outside lane before your exit and never turn right from an inside lane.

question.text: In a traffic circle, who has the right of way?

answer.text: A whole traffic circle counts as one intersection, and vehicles already in the circle have the right of way.

teaching.text: A traffic circle counts as one intersection, and vehicles already in it have the right of way. Remember: circling traffic first.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: A whole traffic circle counts as one intersection, and vehicles already in the circle have the right of way.

question.text: In a traffic circle, who has the right of way and from which lane do you exit?

answer.text: In a traffic circle the vehicles already circulating have the right of way, and you exit only by turning right from the outside lane.

teaching.text: Circling traffic goes first, and exits are right turns from the outside lane. Remember: circlers first, outside exits.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: In a traffic circle the vehicles already circulating have the right of way, and you exit only by turning right from the outside lane.

question.text: What does the roundabout-ahead sign mean, and whom do you yield to on entry?

answer.text: A yellow roundabout-ahead sign tells you to slow down, and on entry you yield to any vehicles or bicyclists already circulating.

teaching.text: Slow at the roundabout-ahead sign, and yield to vehicles and bicyclists already circulating. Remember: slow, yield to circulators.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: A yellow roundabout-ahead sign tells you to slow down, and on entry you yield to any vehicles or bicyclists already circulating.

question.text: Do vehicles inside a roundabout yield to approaching cars, and whom do they yield to when exiting?

answer.text: Vehicles inside a roundabout do not yield to those approaching; signal when you exit and yield to pedestrians in the roundabout crosswalk.

teaching.text: Inside, you do not yield to approaching cars; signal out and yield to pedestrians in the crosswalk. Remember: signal out, yield to walkers.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Vehicles inside a roundabout do not yield to those approaching; signal when you exit and yield to pedestrians in the roundabout crosswalk.

question.text: Who yields to whom at a roundabout?

answer.text: Entering roundabout traffic yields to vehicles and bicyclists already inside, while circulating traffic does not yield to approaching cars but does yield to pedestrians when exiting.

teaching.text: Entering traffic yields, circulating traffic continues, and exiting traffic yields to pedestrians. Remember: entering yields, circling continues.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Entering roundabout traffic yields to vehicles and bicyclists already inside, while circulating traffic does not yield to approaching cars but does yield to pedestrians when exiting.

question.text: How far around a single-lane roundabout do you go to turn right, go straight or turn left?

answer.text: In a single-lane roundabout you go a quarter of the way around to turn right, halfway to go straight, three-quarters to turn left, and all the way around for a U-turn.

teaching.text: Single-lane routes: a quarter around for right, half for straight, three-quarters for left, all the way for a U-turn. Remember: quarter, half, three-quarters.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: In a single-lane roundabout you go a quarter of the way around to turn right, halfway to go straight, three-quarters to turn left, and all the way around for a U-turn.

question.text: How do you choose a lane in a multi-lane roundabout?

answer.text: In a multi-lane roundabout, choose your lane from signs and markings before entering: usually the right lane to exit right and the left lane to go straight, turn left or make a U-turn, with no lane changes inside.

teaching.text: In multi-lane roundabouts, choose your lane from signs and markings before entering, and do not change lanes inside. Remember: pick the lane before entering.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: In a multi-lane roundabout, choose your lane from signs and markings before entering: usually the right lane to exit right and the left lane to go straight, turn left or make a U-turn, with no lane changes inside.

question.text: How does turning left differ in single-lane and multi-lane roundabouts?

answer.text: In a single-lane roundabout three-quarters of the way around replaces a left turn, while in a multi-lane roundabout the left lane is typically used for straight, left and U-turn movements.

teaching.text: Single-lane left turns go three-quarters around, while multi-lane left turns typically use the left lane. Remember: three-quarters, or the left lane.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: In a single-lane roundabout three-quarters of the way around replaces a left turn, while in a multi-lane roundabout the left lane is typically used for straight, left and U-turn movements.

question.text: What should you do in a roundabout when an emergency vehicle comes through?

answer.text: Never enter a roundabout while an emergency vehicle with lights and siren is going through; if you are already inside, exit first and then pull over.

teaching.text: Never enter while an emergency vehicle passes through; if inside, exit first, then pull over. Remember: exit first, then pull over.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Never enter a roundabout while an emergency vehicle with lights and siren is going through; if you are already inside, exit first and then pull over.

question.text: Should drivers pass bicyclists in a roundabout, and where should pedestrians cross?

answer.text: Drivers should not pass a bicyclist inside a roundabout, and pedestrians should use the marked crosswalks around the outside rather than cutting through the middle.

teaching.text: Do not pass bicyclists inside a roundabout, and pedestrians use the outside crosswalks. Remember: no passing bikes inside.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Drivers should not pass a bicyclist inside a roundabout, and pedestrians should use the marked crosswalks around the outside rather than cutting through the middle.

hooks_spoken: Look, signal and sound the horn before passing, and give two feet of clearance.
When someone passes you, move right and never speed up.
recap.narration_text: Time for a quick review of passing safely. Look, signal and sound the horn before passing, and give two feet of clearance. When someone passes you, move right and never speed up. Keep these ideas handy as you practice.

hooks_spoken: Passing on the right is banned except in the listed cases.
On three lanes, pass only in a center lane marked your way.
recap.narration_text: Time for a quick review of passing on the right. Passing on the right is banned except in the listed cases. On three lanes, pass only in a center lane marked your way. Keep these ideas handy as you practice.

hooks_spoken: Park fifteen feet from a hydrant and twenty-five feet from a cross street curb line.
Near a fire, keep a block away in town and four hundred feet outside.
recap.narration_text: Time for a quick review of parking rules. Park fifteen feet from a hydrant and twenty-five feet from a cross street curb line. Near a fire, keep a block away in town and four hundred feet outside. Keep these ideas handy as you practice.

hooks_spoken: Check behind, look over the right shoulder, and back at ten or slower.
recap.narration_text: Time for a quick review of backing. Check behind, look over the right shoulder, and back at ten or slower. Keep these ideas handy as you practice.

hooks_spoken: Inside goes first, then the vehicle on the right, and left turners wait.
Slow down near intersections, even with the right of way.
recap.narration_text: Time for a quick review of intersections and right of way. Inside goes first, then the vehicle on the right, and left turners wait. Slow down near intersections, even with the right of way. Keep these ideas handy as you practice.

hooks_spoken: Circling traffic has the right of way, and you exit right from the outside lane.
At a roundabout, entering traffic yields to traffic already inside.
recap.narration_text: Time for a quick review of traffic circles and roundabouts. Circling traffic has the right of way, and you exit right from the outside lane. At a roundabout, entering traffic yields to traffic already inside. Keep these ideas handy as you practice.

hooks_spoken: Single-lane roundabouts: a quarter right, half straight, three-quarters left.
Never enter a roundabout while an emergency vehicle is coming through.
recap.narration_text: Time for a quick review of roundabout routes and special users. Single-lane roundabouts: a quarter right, half straight, three-quarters left. Never enter a roundabout while an emergency vehicle is coming through. Keep these ideas handy as you practice.
